sections.text: Why Body Fat Percentage Matters More Than Weight
Two people can weigh the same but have completely different health profiles. The difference? Body composition.

Body fat percentage tells you how much of your weight is fat versus lean tissue (muscle, bone, organs, water). It's a far better health indicator than the scale because it reveals what your weight is actually made of. A person at **20% body fat** is  different from someone at **35% body fat**, even at the same weight.
The U. S. Navy circumference method is one of the simplest and most validated tape-measure techniques.

You take a few body measurements — neck, abdomen (for men), or waist and hip (for women) — and plug them into a formula. No expensive equipment, no appointments. The standard error is about **±2–3%** compared to hydrostatic weighing.
For the most accurate results, measure in the morning before eating, use a non-stretchable tape, and have someone else take the measurements.

For men, the formula uses neck and abdomen circumference. For women, it uses neck, waist, and hip. The key measurement is the difference between your trunk and neck — this correlates strongly with total body density. Take each measurement 2–3 times and use the average for the best accuracy. Don't measure after a workout: water loss can give falsely low readings.
How to Improve Your Body Composition

items: Prioritize protein. Aim for **1.6–2.2 g per kg** of body weight daily to preserve muscle during fat loss.
Lift weights, don't just do cardio. Resistance training signals your body to keep muscle while losing fat.
Create a moderate calorie deficit. **300–500 calories below TDEE** targets fat without triggering muscle loss.
Sleep at least **7 hours** per night. Poor sleep increases cortisol and ghrelin, making fat loss harder.
Track trends, not daily numbers. Body fat changes slowly — measure every 2–4 weeks and look for direction over time.
